result: In 181 post-COVID syndrome patients vs 155 fully recovered controls (adjusted for age, BMI, smoking, education, sex, hospitalisation), PCS patients scored lower on all cognitive domains, though hardly clinically significant, with processing speed most affected and larger deficits in those infected early in the pandemic.
reason: Same measure (processing speed deficit) but in long COVID rather than ME/CFS, so a long COVID extension, not an independent replication

result: In 56 ME patients vs 16 controls, the urine-to-plasma ratio of soluble SMPDL3B and renal clearance were lower, plasma SMPDL3B correlated inversely with 1,5-anhydroglucitol and clearance, and alterations were stronger in women.
reason: Measures soluble SMPDL3B but adds a renal/podocyte mechanism and sex difference rather than re-testing increased plasma shedding in an independent cohort; small control group

result: On invasive CPET oxygen-pathway analysis (11 ME/CFS, 15 PASC, 11 controls), peak VO2 was reduced and skeletal muscle O2 diffusion was the most impaired step; normalising it alone would raise VO2 by 34.7% in ME/CFS (p=0.06) and 66% in PASC (p=0.008).
reason: Supports the peripheral extraction limit and localises it to muscle diffusion, but the ME/CFS arm is tiny and modelled, so extends rather than replicates

result: In 15 PASC patients vs 11 controls on invasive CPET, peak VO2 was reduced with skeletal muscle O2 diffusion the most impaired parameter; normalising it would raise VO2 by 66% (p=0.008).
reason: Independent invasive CPET cohort in long COVID showing impaired peripheral O2 extraction, same direction as the finding

result: In RECOVER-Adult (2662 infected aged 60+ and 7549 aged 18-59, plus controls), the adjusted odds of a Long COVID index score of 12 or more were higher at age 40-49 than 18-39 (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.21-1.61), and ageing altered the prevalence and symptom pattern of Long COVID.
reason: Studies age and long COVID symptom index, not new ME/CFS incidence after infection; no atlas finding covers age effects on long COVID prevalence

result: An ALE meta-analysis of 46 neuroimaging studies (2603 people) across conditions with high fatigue found a frontal-striatal-limbic, frontal-cingulate and parietal fatigue network (lateral frontal, cingulate, insula, thalamus, precuneus, caudate).
reason: Transdiagnostic pooling of fatigue activation studies, not reward-task fMRI in ME/CFS; same topic only

result: In 34 PCC patients vs 36 recovered controls, controls improved more than patients on repeated processing-speed tests (coding, partial eta squared .17; Color-Word speed composite p=.031, partial eta squared .08), indicating performance fatigability, with no correlation between performance, perceived and trait fatigue.
reason: Same domain (processing speed) and adds within-session performance fatigability in long COVID
